title: Protecting Your Hearing
hook: Noise-induced hearing loss is permanent — once those tiny inner-ear cells die, they don't grow back. The good news: it's almost entirely preventable.
key_points: Loud noise can permanently damage hearing, and the damage doesn't heal.
Both how loud a sound is and how long you're exposed determine the risk.
Lower the volume, take breaks, and step away from the loudest spots.
Use earplugs or earmuffs at concerts, sporting events, and with power tools.
Ringing or muffled hearing after noise is a warning sign worth heeding.
content_html: Hearing loss from loud noise is one of those harms that feels abstract until it's done — and by then it can't be undone. The cells in your inner ear that turn sound into signals your brain understands don't regenerate once they're damaged.
extra_html: The NIDCD explains that noise-induced hearing loss depends on both how loud a sound is and how long you're around it, so a brief blast or steady loud noise over hours can each take a toll. Because the damage is permanent, prevention is the whole game. The practical moves are simple: turn the volume down, give your ears quiet breaks, and put distance between yourself and the loudest sources. At concerts, sporting events, or while using power tools and yard equipment, foam earplugs or earmuffs make a real difference. Treat warning signs seriously, too — ringing in the ears or muffled hearing after loud exposure means your ears took a hit, and persistent symptoms are worth raising with a clinician.

source.name: U.S. National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH)

related.title: Protecting Your Eyes
related.hook: Some of the most serious eye diseases, like glaucoma, steal sight silently with no early symptoms. A regular eye exam is often the only way to catch them in time.

related.title: Why Regular Checkups Matter
related.hook: The whole point of a checkup is to catch trouble while it's still quiet — before symptoms show up and while it's easiest to treat.

related.title: That Ringing in Your Ears Can Be an Early Warning
related.hook: Hearing loss rarely arrives as silence. It often shows up first as ringing in the ears or a struggle to follow conversation in a noisy room — signs worth heeding early.

flashcards.prompt: What two factors most determine the risk of noise-induced hearing loss?

choices.text: How loud the sound is and how long you're exposed
Your age and your eye color
The time of day and the weather

flashcards.explanation_html: Risk rises with both the loudness of a sound and the length of exposure — loud sounds for long periods are the most damaging.

flashcards.prompt: Can noise-induced hearing loss be reversed?
flashcards.back_html: No. The inner-ear cells that loud noise destroys do not grow back, so the loss is permanent — but it is largely preventable.
